implementation_notes: The standard library has no general timeout combinator, so the idiomatic realization is the async runtime's: tokio::time::timeout(duration, future) polls the wrapped future and returns Err(Elapsed) once the duration has elapsed, cancelling the work by dropping the future - no deregistration or cleanup is required, and into_inner() recovers the original future. Because the future is polled before the deadline is checked, a future that never yields can complete past the deadline without an error. Outside a runtime the closest std primitives are Receiver::recv_timeout(Duration) and thread parking, which cover channels and parks rather than arbitrary calls, so the hand-built timer is replaced by the runtime rather than by syntax.
pitfalls: Drop-based cancellation does not stop blocking code: a future that calls a blocking function only reaches a poll boundary after it returns, so the timeout fires late.
A future that never yields can exceed the duration and still return Ok - the deadline is checked between polls, not during them.
Dropping the Timeout discards in-flight work without rolling it back: if the callee already applied the effect, a retry can duplicate it, so idempotency is part of the timeout decision.
The function panics if no timer is available: the runtime must be built with time enabled (Builder::enable_time), and a timer created outside the runtime also panics.
